seo.title: Karmic tail 15 14 8 compatibility: the Pygmalion story
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 14 8 compatibility: The Devil, Temperance and Justice, with The Tower at the centre of every such couple. A story of two people who sculpt each other.

title: Karmic tail 15-14-8 in compatibility: a couple who sculpt each other
short: The three numbers 15-14-8 in compatibility are The Devil, Temperance and Justice, and every couple with this tail has The Tower at the centre of its matrix. This is the Pygmalion story told for two: the couple is drawn together by the wish to make each other their own, the road runs through a slow mutual recasting, and the main task is to see in the partner not one's own handiwork but a separate person with a design of their own. The Tower at the centre is the moment when the invented image collapses and a living person turns out to be underneath.

sections.h2: First clue: a middle that one person never has
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two ends: it is added up from the partners' middles. A personal matrix follows a different rule: the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task. By that formula 15 and 8 would give 23 → 5, The Hierophant, and that personal tail, 15-5-8, exists. One person never has the tail 15-14-8.

Running through every date since 1900 shows where the fourteen comes from. The tail 15-14-8 arises from a single combination of personal tails: one partner has 6-5-17, the other 9-9-18. That holds for one hundred per cent of such couples. The cards add up in pairs, and in our reading each sum is a small story:

ul: **The Lovers of one and The Hermit of the other give The Devil.** The wish for union plus the habit of solitude: the love of a recluse who makes himself a beloved.

**The Hierophant of one and The Hermit of the other give Temperance.** The teacher is there — The Hierophant stands in one partner's personal tail. But in the couple he is blended with The Hermit, and instead of a lectern there are two cups.
**The Star of one and The Moon of the other give 35, that is, Justice.** The ideal and the imagination are laid on the two pans of the scales.
**The Chariot of one and The Hermit of the other give The Tower at the centre.** Triumph plus withdrawal — and a fall.

paragraphs: One more clue is The Hermit. In one partner's numbers he stands three times: at the entry and the middle of the personal tail and at the centre of the personal chart. So in the couple's sums he appears three times — at the entry, in the middle and at the centre. A person with their own lamp, used to their own company, meets a person with The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle and The Chariot at the centre. This is not a portrait and not a casting of roles: the numbers speak of the themes each brings into the couple, not of who is right.
Both personal tails are rare: 6-5-17 falls to about one date in 57, 9-9-18 to one in 50. Hence the rarity of the couple's tail: about one couple in 1,419 has it (0.07%), and it ranks 86th of 97.

sections.h2: Ovid: a statue no woman could be born like
paragraphs: The best-known story of a man who made himself a beloved is in the tenth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses (X, 243–297). Orpheus sings it, and it comes straight after two short tales of Cyprus: the Cerastae, who had horns growing on their foreheads, and the Propoetides, the first women to sell their bodies, who were turned to stone. Horns and stone, right at the threshold.

Pygmalion had seen the Propoetides and, in Henry Riley's 1851 prose translation, "he lived a single life without a wife, and for a long time was without a partner of his bed". A hermit. From snow-white ivory he carved a woman and gave her a form "qua femina nasci nulla potest" — in Riley's words, "a beauty with which no woman can be born". And he fell in love with his own work.

Ovid then describes the love of a maker for his piece with details that anyone will recognise who has ever loved their dream of a person more than the person. Pygmalion touches the statue and will not admit to himself that it is ivory. "He gives it kisses, and fancies that they are returned." He is afraid his fingers will leave a bruise on her. He brings presents: shells, smooth pebbles, little birds, flowers, amber — the "tears of the Heliades" — rings, necklaces, earrings. He dresses her, lays her on purple coverlets and "calls her the companion of his bed".

At the feast of Venus he does not dare to ask for the statue itself: he prays for a wife and "did not dare to say 'this ivory maid,' but 'like to this statue of ivory.'" Venus understands. At home the ivory grows warm under his hand: "The pressed ivory becomes soft, and losing its hardness, yields to the fingers, and gives way, just as Hymettian wax grows soft in the sun, and being worked with the fingers is turned into many shapes, and becomes pliable by the very handling." The girl who has come alive blushes and, "raising her timorous eyes towards the light of day, she sees at once her lover and the heavens." For the first time she has a gaze of her own — and there Ovid leaves her. What she thinks of her maker the poet never says. She has no name either: the statue would be called Galatea only in the eighteenth century.

The three moves of this story are the three cards of the tail. To make a person to one's own measure and love one's own handiwork is The Devil. To soften the ivory not by force but by warmth and repetition, until the material becomes "pliable by the very handling", is Temperance. The girl who looks for herself for the first time is the beginning of Justice: the second one now has an opinion of the first.

In Riley's English prose translation of 1851 this fable is followed by an "Explanation": the story is most probably an allegory of a man of virtuous principles who "took a great deal of care in training the mind and conduct of a young female", kept her from the prevailing vices and then made her his wife. Some sixty years later Bernard Shaw put that allegory on the stage — and asked what Ovid leaves unsaid.

sections.h2: Shaw: a deal for a shilling
paragraphs: Shaw's Pygmalion was first performed in 1913 in Vienna, in German, and in the spring of 1914 in London, with Herbert Beerbohm Tree as Higgins and Mrs Patrick Campbell as Eliza.

It all begins with a deal, and in it each wants something from the other. The flower girl Eliza Doolittle comes to Henry Higgins, professor of phonetics, in Wimpole Street to buy lessons: she wants to be "a lady in a flower shop" and offers a shilling an hour. Higgins works out that this is two-fifths of her day's income and declares it "the biggest offer I ever had". Colonel Pickering bets the expenses of the whole experiment. Higgins catches fire: "I shall make a duchess of this draggletailed guttersnipe." Eliza's father leaves with five pounds, and later Higgins says of her: "She doesn't belong to him. I paid him five pounds for her."

Higgins's mother, having listened to her son and Pickering, calls them "a pretty pair of babies, playing with your live doll". Higgins and Pickering talk over each other about what they do: teaching Eliza, dressing Eliza and, in Higgins's own words, "inventing new Elizas". Two men are inventing new Elizas while the real one sits beside them.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: a common language that belongs to one
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The point lies on the line of tasks, so the same wish also becomes resistance. In the tail 15-14-8 it holds The Devil, the card of a strong bond and of unfreedom. Lisovskaya's closing thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple: nobody belongs to anybody.

In Pygmalion the common language is literal. Higgins gives Eliza his language — vowels, intonation, words — and in the last act she says: **"I am a child in your country. I have forgotten my own language, and can speak nothing but yours."** This is what The Devil means at the point of the common language: the language two people speak turns out to be the language of one.

In a living couple it looks peaceful, even tender. One brings into the union their pet words, tastes, music, their way of arguing, and a year later the other catches themselves using someone else's phrases. "We don't wear that sort of thing." "This is how we go on holiday." "That's not like you." Presents become corrections: a course, a new wardrobe, a gym pass, a book "you really ought to read". In Ovid the presents go to the statue: they are given not to a person but to an image. In the plus this is passion and growth, two people who can honestly say "we made each other". In the minus each holds the other by what they have put into them.

Shaw sees that both hold the chain. Higgins remakes Eliza, and over the months she becomes indispensable: she knows where his things are, remembers his appointments, brings his slippers. In the last act he tells her what Lisovskaya would list in the minus of the fifteenth energy: "You call me a brute because you couldn't buy a claim on me by fetching my slippers and finding my spectacles." One currency is creation, the other is service. **Both buy a claim on a person.**

On the night after the ball Eliza asks a question that could stand as the epigraph to this tail: "Do my clothes belong to me or to Colonel Pickering?… All I want to know is whether anything belongs to me." She hands back the hired jewels and takes off the ring Higgins bought her in Brighton. He dashes the ring into the fireplace. When he has gone, slamming the door, Eliza goes down on her knees by the hearth to look for the ring. A bond that is renounced aloud is held on to by hand.

Another minus of The Devil in Lisovskaya is silence about one's own wishes. For five acts Eliza talks about slippers, dresses and the bet, and only at the end says what she wants: "I want a little kindness." For a 15-14-8 couple this is the first work at the entry: to say the wish out loud rather than wait for the other to sculpt it. Wen links The Devil with "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification", and Higgins promises a duchess "in six months—in three if she has a good ear and a quick tongue". At the entry the couple wants results now. The middle of the tail will teach it another kind of time.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: two people chained to each other
paragraphs: On Waite's Devil a male and a female figure are chained to a ring in front of the altar. Wen opens her description of the same card with the words "The Lovers from Key 6 are chained by a horned beast". In the couple's tail it comes out exactly so: The Lovers of one plus The Hermit of the other give The Devil.

Waite himself opens his description of the design with an unusual word: it is "an accommodation, mean or harmony, between several motives". The same word, accommodation, ends his divinatory list for Temperance: "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation." Waite's Devil is a middle too, only a counterfeit one. Higgins describes such a middle better than any commentator: **"One wants to go north and the other south; and the result is that both have to go east, though they both hate the east wind."**

The second detail: he who is exalted above the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". In Pygmalion the master depends no less: "I have grown accustomed to your voice and appearance. I like them, rather." When Eliza hands back the jewels, Higgins thrusts them into his pockets, "unconsciously decorating himself with the protruding ends of the chains" — so runs Shaw's stage direction.

The third detail is almost a hint for the couple's tail. In the part of his book on older packs, Waite notes that in Papus's version the small demons of The Devil are replaced by "naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other", and adds: "The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." Nobody stands above such a pair. The chain is the two of them.

Of The Tower Waite writes that "there is a sense in which the catastrophe is a reflection from the previous card" — The Devil: one card is concerned with "the fall into the material and animal state", the other signifies "destruction on the intellectual side". In the tail 15-14-8 The Devil stands at the entry and The Tower at the centre, and Waite draws the link between them himself. As for Temperance, in his words "it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures" — the very work for which this couple walks the middle.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Temperance: two cups instead of a lectern
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. Our reading: the middle shows how the couple travels from the wish at the entry to the main task. In the tail 15-14-8 the road runs through Temperance, the card of measure and blending.

Here the arithmetic of the first clue is at work. One person on this road would pass through The Hierophant: teacher, rule, pupil. Shaw's play is built as a course of lessons, but by the end the lessons run both ways. Eliza tells Pickering that her real education began not with phonetics but on the day he called her "Miss Doolittle". Higgins admits: "I have learnt something from your idiotic notions: I confess that humbly and gratefully." And Eliza throws at him: "If you can preach, I can teach." **In a 15-14-8 couple the teacher is not abolished but diluted:** each pours their own into the common cup.

The best scene of Temperance in progress is the third act, the at-home at Higgins's mother's. Eliza has strict orders to keep to two subjects, the weather and how everybody is. She delivers the weather like a meteorological bulletin, her vowels are flawless, and the content comes straight from Lisson Grove: her aunt, she insists, was done in for the sake of a new straw hat — "them as pinched it done her in". Two waters are poured into one cup but have not yet blended. On her way out Eliza drops "Not bloody likely" — at the London premiere in 1914 that line brought the house down.

In her example about work, Wen describes Temperance as fusing what a person already has with what is expected of them: "it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand". For the couple this turns the whole story round. Its middle is not to remake a person but to fuse what both already have. Higgins describes his own work as "filling up the deepest gulf that separates class from class and soul from soul". Temperance is a bridge over that gulf, not the moving of one bank onto the other.

In Ovid the ivory comes alive not under the chisel but under a warm hand, and the wax, as he puts it, becomes pliable by the very handling. Time is an ally in this middle: the blend is not made in three months.

In life the middle of this couple is a long blending. Whose holidays, whose cooking, whose weekend rhythm, whose friends at the table. In the plus, after a few years the two speak a third language that neither had before. In the minus, as Lisovskaya puts it, one always gives way while the other does not even notice. From outside it looks like compromise; inside, both are walking into the east wind. Another minus of Temperance is perfectionism and dependence on other people's opinion: in Shaw the exam is set by guests at a society party, and Eliza passes it so brilliantly that everyone forgets about her.

Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fourteenth energy not to jump to conclusions about the partner, not to shift their own fears and wishes onto them, and to know how to wait for the right moment. For the tail 15-14-8 this is a rule against Pygmalion: not to sculpt the other after one's own fear and one's own wish.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Tower: the night after the ball
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two, what is inside and not on show. Every couple with the tail 15-14-8 has The Tower there: The Chariot of one and The Hermit of the other. In Lisovskaya The Tower in the plus means trials the couple goes through hand in hand, after which the union is stronger; in the minus, the collapse of an invented image of the partner.

The fourth act of Pygmalion is The Tower almost word for word. Midnight, the laboratory in Wimpole Street, Eliza in diamonds after the garden party, the dinner and the opera. The bet is won. Pickering congratulates Higgins on his triumph — that is The Chariot. Higgins answers with relief: "Thank God it's over!" The whole thing has been a bore, and now he can go to bed at last "without dreading tomorrow" — that is The Hermit going back into himself. Nobody notices Eliza. When Higgins, outside the door, asks what the devil he has done with his slippers, she hurls them at him: "There are your slippers. And there. Take your slippers; and may you never have a day's luck with them!"

Both images collapse. Higgins sees not his handiwork but a person with claws, and refuses to believe it: "It's only imagination." Eliza sees that to him she is "not so much as them slippers", and asks what nobody thought of at the entry: **"What's to become of me?"** The Chariot's triumph plus The Hermit's solitude — and The Tower stands at the centre.

This Tower has its material too. Pygmalion worked in ivory, and the "ivory tower" is an old image of seclusion. In the Song of Songs the beloved's neck is "as a tower of ivory", and in 1837 Sainte-Beuve called the poet Alfred de Vigny's retreat his tour d'ivoire. A hermit carving his ideal alone lives exactly there. The Tower at the centre of this couple is a closed world for two, where an image is easy to create and hard to keep in daylight.

Shaw understood the force of this card. In his sequel he writes that nothing could alter the relations of Eliza and Higgins but "some emergency or calamity great enough to break down all likes and dislikes, and throw them both back on their common humanity" — and adds at once: "and may they be spared any such trial!" The Tower at the centre does not promise calamity. It says something else: in this couple the truth comes through a shaking, and after it the two can see each other as people.

In the last act Higgins finds the word himself. Five minutes ago, he tells Eliza, "you were like a millstone round my neck. Now you're a tower of strength". The millstone round the neck is The Devil. The tower of strength is The Tower lived through together: after the fall, an equal stands before him.

sections.h2: Main task — Justice: on what terms
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is D, and Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. In the tail 15-14-8 it is Justice, arcanum 8 (XI in Waite's numbering).

In Pygmalion the question of this card is asked by Higgins's mother back in the third act, when nobody wants to hear it: **"But on what terms? Is she a servant? If not, what is she?"** At the entry the couple had a wish. It had no terms. The main task is to agree on them after the fact.

Eliza's answer in the last act is the best definition of Justice for this couple: "the difference between a lady and a flower girl is not how she behaves, but how she's treated." Higgins replies with his own definition: the great secret is "having the same manner for all human souls" and behaving as if in Heaven, "where there are no third-class carriages". "He treats a flower girl as if she was a duchess," Eliza says of Pickering. "And I treat a duchess as if she was a flower girl," Higgins replies. Formally he is just: he is rude to everyone alike. Eliza answers with a line that leaves nothing to argue about: **"I notice that you don't notice me."**

This is the minus of the eighth energy in Lisovskaya: measuring everything by oneself and not noticing what hurts the partner. The justice of this couple is not one rule for everyone but attention to one person. The same scales for all do not yet mean that the person beside you has been weighed on them.

Towards the end Shaw shows the other pan as well. "And you may throw me out tomorrow if I don't do everything you want me to?" Eliza asks. "Yes; and you may walk out tomorrow if I don't do everything YOU want me to." For the first time the two have equal terms: both have the right to leave — which means staying can also be a free choice.

Roman jurists defined justice as the constant will to render to each what is due to them: suum cuique. Eliza's question from the night after the ball — what belongs to me — is the same question. And she answers it herself: "You can't take away the knowledge you gave me." What was given becomes one's own.

The main task is added up from two personal ones: The Star of one partner and The Moon of the other. In Waite the figure of The Star "expresses eternal youth and beauty", and The Moon "represents life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". Pygmalion's statue is exactly that: eternal beauty seen by the imagination. The sum gives the scales. Our reading: the couple's task is to lay the ideal on one pan and what the imagination has filled in on the other, and see what a living person weighs.

In daily life the justice of this couple is tested by questions that are awkward to ask. Who decided the other needed that degree — they themselves, or the one who "knows better"? Whose plan was it: the move, the renovation, the wedding for a hundred guests? Who apologised after the last quarrel, and who thinks there is nothing to apologise for, because "I only wanted what was best"? Lisovskaya sees in the minus of the eighth energy an over-responsibility that turns into control, and advises the couple to set limits on advice and help and to let go of idealising the partner. For a couple who sculpt each other this is a rule of the workshop: **help ends where someone else's design begins**.

The conversation about Freddy, who writes to Eliza "twice and three times a day", is a short summary of the whole tail. "Can he MAKE anything of you? That's the point," says Higgins. "Perhaps I could make something of him," Eliza answers. "But I never thought of us making anything of one another; and you never think of anything else. I only want to be natural." The Devil asks who will make whom. Justice asks whether one may simply be.

sections.h2: Pygmalion or Michelangelo: what psychologists measured
paragraphs: This story has a scientific sequel. In 1999 the American psychologists Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult and their co-authors described the "Michelangelo phenomenon": close partners sculpt each other. How one sees the other and treats them gradually becomes part of the other's character.

The name comes from the sculptor. Michelangelo held that the figure is already enclosed in the block: his sonnet 151 says that the best artist has no idea that a single marble does not contain "col suo superchio" — within its excess (our translation). The chisel only removes what is superfluous. In Rusbult's words, Michelangelo "described sculpting as a process whereby the artist releases an ideal figure from the block of stone in which it slumbers", and a good partner works the same way: sees in the other that person's own ideal — who they themselves dream of becoming — and helps that figure emerge.

In one study, married partners were filmed discussing a goal that mattered to one of them, and four months later the researchers asked whether it had been reached. Those whose partners helped and supported them in the conversation, rather than criticising, were more likely to have achieved their goals.

Rusbult has a name for the opposite case too — the "Pygmalion phenomenon": a partner who perceives and treats the other "in ways that are consistent with the partner's ideal self (irrespective of the target's ideal self)". In a 2009 review the authors write that it is "negatively associated with diverse indices of personal and couple well-being", and conclude: **"it is unwise to foist one's ideal self representations onto others."** Ironically, the notion of the "ideal self" on which this whole line of work rests was taken from a psychologist named Higgins — E. Tory Higgins, author of self-discrepancy theory (1987).

The tail 15-14-8 fits into these two names. The entry is Pygmalion: sculpting in one's own image. The main task is Michelangelo: seeing the figure already present in the other. The middle is the work of the chisel, and it takes time: the same review says the sculptor "must not only understand the ideal form slumbering in the block, but must also understand the block per se – what possibilities are inherent in the block, and what flaws must be circumvented".
The argument about how this story ends has gone on for more than a hundred years — and it resembles the choice the tail 15-14-8 puts before a couple.

Ovid's ending is happy and brief: the goddess attends the wedding, nine moons later Paphos is born, and the island will take that name. In Shaw, Eliza leaves for her father's wedding, while Higgins, left alone, is sure she will buy him a ham, a Stilton cheese and gloves all the same. In 1914 Beerbohm Tree, the first Higgins, added a romantic gesture at the end without the author's knowledge. The exchange with Shaw became an anecdote: "My ending makes money; you ought to be grateful." — "Your ending is damnable; you ought to be shot."

In 1916 Shaw added a sequel to the play, "What Happened Afterwards". Eliza marries Freddy; they open a flower shop with Pickering's money and attend bookkeeping classes and even the London School of Economics: "business, like phonetics, has to be learned". Eliza spars with Higgins for the rest of her life. The sequel's last sentence: **"Galatea never does quite like Pygmalion: his relation to her is too godlike to be altogether agreeable."**

The cinema disagreed with Shaw. In the 1938 film, for whose screenplay Shaw and his co-writers won an Oscar, Eliza comes back, and Higgins, his back turned, asks about his slippers. The musical My Fair Lady (1956) took that ending, and its last line is: "Eliza, where the devil are my slippers?" The devil is in the last line. If the work of Justice is skipped, the story returns to its entry: to the slippers, to service, to The Devil.

The tail does not choose the couple's ending. Staying together or parting is not its question; its question is on what terms. The same couple may go back to the slippers, or stay as equals — and then each finds their own slippers.

sections.h2: The couple's values: what grows out of the workshop
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, the answer to what the union exists for. Couples with the tail 15-14-8 most often have The Empress there (54.1%), then The World (32.2%) and The Hanged Man (13.7%).

For Lisovskaya The Empress means fruitfulness, abundance and growth, and in money her advice is to grow through shared goals in such a way that each partner has their own fulfilment. Ovid ends his story with a birth; Shaw, with a flower shop that did not pay for a long time and then began to prosper, and the former flower girl became its owner. The value of such a couple is what grows when the workshop turns into a garden: a shared venture in which each has their own bed.

The World means freedom and the wide world. "If I can't have kindness, I'll have independence," says Eliza. For a couple with The World among its values, each partner's independence is not a threat to the union but its aim.

The Hanged Man is a view turned upside down: the pupil suddenly announces that she will teach. For a couple with The Hanged Man the value lies in changing places from time to time and looking at the union from the other's side.

If the middle were counted by the personal formula, it would be 15 + 8 = 23 → 5. But a couple's points are added point by point: the middle from the middles, which gives 14. The couple's values in this example are 3, The Empress.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 15-14-8 tail

ul: **Saying wishes out loud.** Not waiting for the other to guess and sculpt them: it took Eliza five acts to say one sentence, "I want a little kindness".
**Asking about the other's ideal instead of offering one's own.** "Who do you want to become?" before "that would suit you". This is the difference between Pygmalion and Michelangelo.
**Checking presents and advice.** Who is the present for — the person or the image? A course, a book, a new haircut are good when the one receiving them wants them.
**Blending slowly.** A couple's common language takes years to form. If the same one always gives way, it is not Temperance but the east wind.
**Talking after a triumph.** A wedding, a move, a thesis defended, the end of a renovation — that is the night after the ball. It is the moment to ask what happens now to each of the two.
**Agreeing on terms.** Who is responsible for what, and what belongs to whom. The right to leave and the right to stay belong to both.
**Owning one's share.** Justice begins with the words "I sculpted too", not with "I only wanted what was best".

paragraphs: If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in the relationship, that is not a task of the tail to be "worked through" but a reason to call the local emergency number or a crisis line and to seek help from people close to you and from professionals.

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** What the couple wants together: a bond in which each "makes" the other. The common language of two easily becomes the language of one.
**Middle of the task — 14, Temperance.** The road is walked not by command but by measure: the two blend like water from two cups, and both change — slowly, like wax under warm fingers.

**Main task — 8, Justice.** To give each their own: their own goals, their own voice, their own right to leave and to stay. In the minus, measuring the partner by oneself and not noticing what hurts them.

intro: The riddle of this tail is written in its arithmetic. A middle of 14 is impossible in a personal matrix: a person walking alone from The Devil to Justice would pass through The Hierophant, the card of the teacher. A couple passes through Temperance. There is a teacher in such a couple, but in the sum he dissolves. What follows is the evidence: the site engine's numbers, Ovid, Bernard Shaw, Waite, Wen, Yuliana Lisovskaya and the psychologists who measured how partners sculpt each other.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-14-8 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Devil as the entry to the task, Temperance in the middle and Justice as the main task, and The Tower always at the centre of the matrix. The couple is drawn together by a strong wish to make each other their own, the road runs through mutual measure, and what it has to learn is justice: seeing the partner as a separate person with their own goals and rights.

faq.q: Why does the tail 15-14-8 never occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task: 15 + 8 = 23 → 5, which would give the tail 15-5-8. In a couple's matrix the middle is added up from the partners' middles, here 5 + 9, which gives 14.

faq.q: Does The Devil at the entry mean the couple is dependent?
faq.a: No. The card does not establish dependencies or anyone's actions. At the entry point The Devil describes the couple's shared wish: a strong bond in which two people change each other. In the plus it is passion and growth; in the minus, an attempt to hold the other by what has been put into them.

faq.q: Does The Tower at the couple's centre mean a break-up?
faq.a: No, the card does not predict events. The Tower at the centre is a quality of the atmosphere: an invented image of the partner does not last long here, and the truth comes through a shaking. For Lisovskaya, trials gone through together make such a union stronger.

faq.q: How common is the 15-14-8 tail in a couple?
faq.a: About one couple in 1,419 has it (0.07%), which ranks it 86th of the 97 couple tails. It arises from a single combination of personal tails: one partner has 6-5-17, the other 9-9-18.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The method has no other couple tails made of 15, 14 and 8: the order 15-14-8 is the only one.

report: Ovid tells of a sculptor who lived alone, carved a woman out of ivory with "a beauty with which no woman can be born", and fell in love with his own work. Pygmalion kisses the statue, "fancies that they are returned" and brings it shells, rings and necklaces. The presents go not to a person but to an image. The karmic tail 15-14-8 is this story told for two. At the entry stands The Devil: the couple is drawn together by the wish to make each other their own. In the middle stands Temperance: the road runs through a slow mutual recasting. The main task is Justice: to see in the partner not one's own handiwork but a separate person with a design of their own. And at the couple's centre stands The Tower — the moment when the invented image collapses.

report.h3: A common language spoken by one

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: its agreements and its "common language". The Devil stands here, the card of a strong bond and of unfreedom, and the common language of two easily becomes the language of one. In Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion this is said literally: Professor Higgins gives the flower girl Eliza his vowels, his intonation and his words, and in the last act she admits that she has forgotten her own language and can speak nothing but his.

In a living couple it looks peaceful, even tender. One brings their pet words, tastes, music and way of arguing, and a year later the other catches themselves using someone else's phrases: "we don't wear that sort of thing", "we don't do it that way". Presents become corrections — a course, a new wardrobe, a book that simply "must be read". In the plus this is passion and growth, two people who can honestly say "we made each other". In the minus each holds the other by what they have put into them.

Shaw sees that both hold the chain. Higgins remakes Eliza, and she becomes indispensable: she remembers his appointments and brings his slippers. One currency is creation, the other is service. **Both buy a claim on a person.** On the night after the ball Eliza asks who her clothes belong to and then says the main thing: "All I want to know is whether anything belongs to me." Waite writes approvingly of a version of The Devil with a man and a woman "yoked only to each other": nobody stands above such a pair, and the chain is the two of them.

report.h3: The teacher is not abolished but diluted

report: The middle of the tail shows how the couple travels its road. Here stands Temperance, the card of measure and blending: there is a teacher in such a couple, but that voice is blended with the voice of the other, and instead of a lectern there are two cups. Shaw's play is built as a course of lessons, and by the end the lessons run both ways. Higgins admits that he has learnt something from Eliza — "humbly and gratefully". Eliza announces that she will teach herself.

In Ovid the ivory comes alive not under the chisel but under a warm hand: it softens like wax in the sun and becomes "pliable by the very handling". The blend is not made in three months. In the plus, after a few years the two speak a third language that neither had before. In the minus the same one always gives way while the other does not even notice. Higgins described such a middle himself: **"One wants to go north and the other south; and the result is that both have to go east, though they both hate the east wind."**

The fourth act of Pygmalion is The Tower almost word for word. The bet is won, Eliza is still in her diamonds, and Higgins says with relief: "Thank God it's over!" Nobody notices her. When he asks what the devil has become of his slippers, she hurls them at him. Both images collapse: he sees not his handiwork but a person with claws, she sees that to him she is "not so much as them slippers". And a question is heard that nobody thought of at the entry: "What's to become of me?"

The Tower at the centre does not promise calamity. It says something else: an invented image does not last long here, the truth comes through a shaking, and after it the two can see each other as people. In the last act Higgins tells Eliza that five minutes ago she hung round his neck like a millstone, and now she is "a tower of strength".

report.h3: Scales that weigh a living person

report: The question of Justice is asked by Higgins's mother, and nobody wants to hear it: "But on what terms? Is she a servant? If not, what is she?" At the entry the couple had a wish and no terms. Eliza's answer is the best definition of this card for such a couple: **"the difference between a lady and a flower girl is not how she behaves, but how she's treated"**. Higgins replies that he has "the same manner for all human souls", and formally he is just: he is rude to everyone alike. Eliza retorts that what she notices is that he does not notice her. This is the minus of Justice: measuring everything by oneself and not seeing what hurts the partner.

Psychologists who study couples have two names for this. The "Michelangelo phenomenon" is when a partner sees in the other that person's own ideal and helps the figure emerge, as a sculptor frees it from the block. The "Pygmalion phenomenon" is when a partner sculpts the other after their own ideal; it is linked to lower well-being for both the person and the couple. The authors' conclusion: "it is unwise to foist one's ideal self representations onto others." For a couple with the tail 15-14-8 this is a rule of the workshop: **help ends where someone else's design begins**.

Shaw ended the sequel to his play with the sentence: "Galatea never does quite like Pygmalion: his relation to her is too godlike to be altogether agreeable." The musical My Fair Lady brought Eliza back to Higgins, and its last line is "Eliza, where the devil are my slippers?" If the work of Justice is skipped, the story returns to its entry: to the slippers, to service, to The Devil. The tail does not choose the couple's ending; its question is on what terms two people stay side by side.

What changes the script: saying wishes out loud instead of waiting for the other to guess; asking about the other's own ideal before saying what would suit them; after every shared triumph, talking about what happens next to each of the two; agreeing on who is responsible for what and what belongs to whom; owning one's share — **"I sculpted too"** instead of "I only wanted what was best". If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in the relationship, that is not a task of the tail but a reason to call a local emergency number or crisis line and to seek help.
